newsitem.title: CHINA: China court jails dissident for nine years.
newsitem.headline: China court jails dissident for nine years.

text.p: A Chinese court has sentenced dissident and former student leader Li Hai to nine years in prison for prying into state secrets, a family member said on Tuesday.
In a trial held behind closed doors, Beijing's Chaoyang District Court convicted Li around December 18, a relative told Reuters by telephone.
"We're very surprised," the relative said, adding that he believed the appeal process had already started.
"Our only hope is in the appeal," he said.
The family has not been allowed to meet Li since he was detained on May 31, 1995.
A Hong Kong-based human rights watchdog quoted family members as saying they doubted the charges because Li was not a civil servant and had no access to state secrets.

Li was first arrested on May 31, 1990, for his role in the 1989 student demonstrations for democracy. He was released six months later and expelled from the philosophy department of the prestigious Beijing University where he was a graduate student.
China jailed dozens of dissidents in 1996 as part of its obsession with stability coupled with the easing foreign pressure on its human rights record, diplomats and human rights activists say.

Authorities jailed 12 better-known dissidents or sent them to labour camps in 1996. Of the 12, former student leader Wang Dan received the harshest sentence -- 11 years -- for conspiring to subvert the government.

Western human rights activists say sending dissidents to labour camps has been increasingly favoured as a way of removing dissidents from circulation without the complications or publicity of a trial.
At least 10 lesser-known political activists have been incarcerated in the northern region of Inner Mongolia. In the southwestern city of Guiyang, another seven to eight dissidents have been jailed.
Two dissidents fled to the United States this year -- former student leader Liu Gang and veteran dissident Wang Xizhe.
